I have farmed these 4.1 mu for 35 years, and I know every corner of this land. Last year my wheat gave me about 480 kg per mu and my maize about 550 kg per mu, so this year I will do the same thing because it did not fail me. After I harvest the maize in autumn, I will run the rotary tiller over the whole field to break up the stalks and make a good seedbed for the wheat. I sow my wheat with an improved variety, about 12.5 kg of seed per mu. For fertilizer, I put down one full bag — 50 kg — of that 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu as base fertilizer before sowing. Then when the wheat turns green in spring, I spread another half-bag, about 25 kg, of urea on top. That is what my neighbor Lao Wang does, and his wheat always looks strong. I water three times: once before winter so the wheat can survive the cold, once at jointing when it shoots up, and once when the grain is filling. I spray herbicide once in early spring, and if I see aphids or rust I spray one more time.

For the summer maize, I plant it right after the wheat comes off the combine, usually within two days because the season is short. I do not till the field again; I just direct-seed into the wheat stubble. I use hybrid seed, about 2.5 kg per mu. At planting I put down 40 kg per mu of the same 15-15-15 compound fertilizer. When the plants are knee-high and throwing the big ear, I top-dress with 25 kg per mu of urea. I irrigate twice if the rain does not come — once when the ears are forming, and once when the grain is filling. I spray herbicide once after sowing, and once for corn borer when I see moths flying at night. I would rather spend a little more on fertilizer than risk losing yield. A bad harvest means I cannot pay for my wife's medicine or my grandson's school fees. Wasting some fertilizer is just money out of my pocket; a bad harvest is a disaster. I do not trust new ideas from outside unless I saw them work on Lao Wang's field first.
